name: Yusuf Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four and in the cow shed by five. I'm the herdsman at Hollins Farm, been there twenty-two years, ninety milking cows plus barley and some grass for silage, and the farm belongs to a family trust that mostly lives in the city. Milking, scraping out, feeding, checking feet, then whatever the manager has on the list, could be drilling, could be fencing. I like the cows, I know every one of them by her walk, and what wears me out is the early starts and a back that's not forty any more.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the farm belongs to a trust. What does that mean for you day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It means I don't own a blade of grass and I live in the tied cottage, the house that comes with the job. If the job goes, the house goes with it, and Maureen and I have never managed to save more than a few weeks of wages. Maureen does the dinners at the village school. Our two are grown and gone, one's a bus driver, one's in a care home kitchen, so it's just the two of us and the dog now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: We'll go through five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Every few years somebody comes round with a new box that's going to change farming, and it ends up in the corner of the shed with a sheet over it. Down the Fleece on a Friday I'd have a laugh about it with the other lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd be a relief. I'm fifty-eight, I've got maybe eight years left before the pension, and I'd rather the ground didn't move under me in those years. The thing that worries me on the farm isn't computers, it's milk price and whether the trust sells up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, I'd keep going. Same shifts, same cows, keep my head down and keep the union subs paid. Maybe I'd let the manager put one of those apps on my phone if he really insisted, but I don't use any of that AI stuff myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, it feels fine. Like an ordinary Tuesday. A bit of me would be smug, I'll admit that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything on the farm today where you've already seen some of this routine automation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's the collars, the ones that tell you when a cow's bulling or off her food, and the manager reads them on his tablet. The collar tells him what I'd have told him anyway, it just doesn't need a cup of tea first. I don't mind them, they've never taken a shift off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things stayed like this, what does the next eight years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, then hand the cottage keys back and hope the council has a little flat for us. The pension is small and I know that. But eight more years of this, my body will hold up if the weather's kind.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads at the pub I told them so, because every new box that's meant to change farming ends up in the corner under a sheet. I'd have a laugh about it.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I've got about eight years left before my pension and I don't want the ground moving under me. My real worries are milk price and whether the trust sells the farm.
S0.do: Keeps working his usual shifts as herdsman and keeps paying his union subs. Lets the manager add apps if he insists but doesn't use AI tools himself.
S0.feel: Settled and a little smug, like an ordinary working day.
S0.quote: The collar tells him what I'd have told him anyway, it just doesn't need a cup of tea first.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf's real fears sit outside technology: the milk price, the trust selling up and the tied cottage that goes with the job. He talks about the cow collars without resentment because they haven't cost him hours. A quiet, steady man who mostly wants the next eight years to be boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said, some of it is already on the farm. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the owners who'll do well out of it and the workers who'll pay, same as always. I'd say it at the union branch meeting and I'd say it to anyone who asked. If machines are going to do the work, then the people who did the work should get something back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think this is the one where I lose the milking. A robot milker on a ninety-cow herd pays for itself in a few years, and I'm the biggest wage on that farm after the manager. They'd keep me for the field work maybe, but on fewer hours, and I'm no good with the computer side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the branch secretary first thing, Pat, and ask what the union's doing about it. I'd start putting twenty a week aside, which is hard, and cancel the TV package. I wouldn't go on a course for the robot, I'll be honest, I don't think I'd learn it at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a stone in my stomach. I'm not panicking, but I'd be watching the manager's face every time the trust's man came down from the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robot milker. Has the manager or the trust ever talked about one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, two winters back, there was a salesman in the yard with brochures. The manager said, ‘Not yet, Yusuf,’ and patted my shoulder, and I've thought about that ‘yet’ ever since. That's the only time it's come up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else around you would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, the young lad who does relief milking on my days off. He's twenty-three and his whole plan is to be a herdsman like me. In this picture there's no herdsman job left for him to grow into.

S1.say: I'd say the owners will do well and the workers will pay, as usual, and I'd say it at the union branch. If machines do the work, the people who did it should get something back.
S1.think: I think this is when I lose the milking, because a robot milker pays for itself and I'm the biggest wage after the manager. They might keep me on fewer hours for field work, but I'm no good with computers.
S1.do: Goes to his union branch secretary straight away to ask what's being done. Starts saving twenty a week and cancels the TV subscription, but says he wouldn't retrain on the robot.
S1.feel: A heavy, steady worry, like a stone in his stomach, without panic.
S1.quote: The manager said, ‘Not yet, Yusuf,’ and patted my shoulder, and I've thought about that ‘yet’ ever since.
S1.fieldNote: The manager's ‘not yet’ two winters ago clearly stuck with him; he's been half expecting a robot milker for a while. He's quick to name owners as the ones who gain and turns to the union by reflex. He rules out retraining himself with no fuss, which is a striking gap next to his concern for the young relief milker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is quite different. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government had better step in, and fast. You can't let a few companies own every machine that does every job and leave the rest of us with nothing. I'd sign every petition, I'd go on the march in town, and I'd say so on the radio phone-in if they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished as a herdsman. Two years is nothing, I'd be sixty, too young for my pension and too old for anyone to hire. If a robot can milk and feed and drive the tractor, the trust doesn't need me or the cottage I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd go to the union and the council about housing, because the house is the thing. I'd ask Maureen to pick up more hours at the school while that's still there. I'd go to my son and ask if we could stay with him for a bit if it came to it, which would kill me to ask, and I'd vote for whoever promised to share out what the machines earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly frightened. I'm not someone who lies awake much, but I would with this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what happens to the cottage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is one more calving season and then a cardboard box on the doorstep. That's the honest answer. Tied cottages go with the job and there's nowhere else in the valley to rent on what we'd have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the robot. If it came to that or no job, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, I'd have to. But I'd be the slowest learner they ever had, and why would they pay me to watch a machine that watches itself. I don't think it'd come to that choice, is the truth.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to step in fast, because a few companies can't own every machine that does every job. I'd sign petitions, march in town and ring the radio phone-in.
S2.think: I think I'm finished as a herdsman, too young for the pension and too old to be hired. If a robot can do the milking, feeding and tractor work, the trust doesn't need me or my cottage.
S2.do: Goes to the union and the council about housing first, and asks his wife to take more hours. Asks his son about staying with him if needed, and votes for whoever promises to share out what machines earn.
S2.feel: Properly frightened, the kind of worry that would keep him awake.
S2.quote: Two years is one more calving season and then a cardboard box on the doorstep.
S2.fieldNote: Housing, not wages, is the centre of his fear: the tied cottage turns a job loss into homelessness. With two years and no savings he sees no move he can make himself, only asks of the union, the council and his son. He'd try the robot work if forced but doesn't believe he'd be kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's add a bit more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before really, but I'd be louder earlier. Five years is long enough that the union and the government have no excuse. I'd say: you can see it coming, so plan for the people, not just the profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still bad for me, but five years gets me to sixty-three. That's close enough to the pension that I'm not completely lost. I'd still lose the cottage, I'm sure of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager straight out, in the first year, what the trust's plan is, so I'm not the last to know. I'd put our name down on the council housing list now, because it's years long. And I'd get Maureen to sort out what pension she's got, because I've never looked at mine properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more like a long ache than a fright. There'd be time to see the ground before you fall on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those three years before it arrives look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Putting our name down, that's the big one. And probably picking up a weekend job at the feed store in town, if they'd still have people working there, just to build something up. Twenty a week for three years isn't much, but it's three years more than we've ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go to your son, in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. Five years, I think we'd manage between the council and the pension. My son's got kids now and a small house. I'd go to him last.

S3.say: I'd say the same as before but louder and earlier, because five years means the union and the government have no excuse. Plan for the people, not just the profits.
S3.think: It's still bad, but five years gets me to sixty-three, close to my pension. I'm sure I'd still lose the tied cottage.
S3.do: Asks the manager about the trust's plans in the first year and puts the family on the council housing list now. Looks for a weekend job at the feed store and starts saving twenty a week.
S3.feel: A long ache rather than a fright, with time to see what's coming.
S3.quote: Twenty a week for three years isn't much, but it's three years more than we've ever had.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years change his plans more than his feelings: he moves from asking for rescue to getting on the housing list and finding a weekend job. He has never looked at his own pension properly, which he admits easily. Still expects to lose the cottage either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly if anyone in charge bothers. Retrain the young ones, share out the money, look after people's homes. I'd keep saying it at the branch, and I'd still be voting the same way I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, ten years gets me to my pension. It's the younger ones I'd worry about, Dev and lads like him. It's a sad thing to say, but the timing would mostly let me off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, mostly. Keep working, keep the subs up, get on the housing list at some point. I'd keep saying no to the AI apps, because I won't need them before I'm done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad more than scared. Sad for the farm and the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty-eight. Where do you see yourself on the day it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the bench outside a council flat with the dog, I hope. I'd hear about the robots at Hollins from the lads and I'd say, ‘They'll never get Daisy's feet right.’ And I'd probably be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the farm itself you'd want to see protected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody should still walk the hedges and know the cows. I don't know who'd pay for that. But it'd be a shame if no one who'd ever stood in that shed at five in the morning was left on the place.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it properly if those in charge bother: retrain young people, share the money and protect people's homes. I'd keep saying it at the union branch.
S4.think: Ten years gets me to my pension, so the timing mostly lets me off. It's the younger ones, like the relief milker Dev, that I'd worry about.
S4.do: Keeps working and paying his union subs, and puts the family on the housing list at some point. Keeps refusing AI apps because he expects to retire before he'd need them.
S4.feel: Sad for the farm and the young people more than scared for himself.
S4.quote: I'd hear about the robots at Hollins from the lads and I'd say, ‘They'll never get Daisy's feet right.’
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Yusuf off the hook personally and his worry turns outward to Dev and the young workers. He pushes housing action back to ‘at some point’, which shows how much more relaxed he is than with two years. There's real grief for the craft of knowing a herd.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. A herdsman without a herd is just a man in a borrowed house. What would help is a law that says if your job goes to a machine, you don't lose your home with it, and a pension you can take at sixty if the work's gone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Maureen. Everyone asks about the farm, but she'd be the one finding the flat and sorting the forms, because I'm useless at that. Somebody should ask the wives what this would cost them.

headlineQuote: A herdsman without a herd is just a man in a borrowed house.
portrait: Yusuf Walsh is a 58-year-old herdsman who has milked ninety cows on a trust-owned farm for twenty-two years and lives in the tied cottage that comes with the job. He has almost no savings, never uses AI tools and has no wish to learn. He leans left, trusts his union and blames owners when machines replace workers. He is calm about a plateau, anxious about a robot milker, and frightened by fast AGI because losing the job means losing his home. With ten years' warning he mostly expects to reach his pension and worries more for the young workers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because with two years he'd lose the job and the tied cottage before he reaches his pension.
whatWouldHelp: A law so people don't lose their homes when their job goes to a machine, and a pension that can be taken at sixty if the work has gone.
